headline: A CMP enrollment left waiting can be picked up by a later process instead of started again.
summary:
A certification authority that answers waiting can take hours to decide, and pki.cmp.session held the whole exchange in memory: its transaction identifier, its nonce chain, and the key it asked to have certified. When the poll budget ran out the session returned poll-timeout and that state was gone, so a caller whose process ended had no way to collect a certificate that was later issued for a request it had already made.

A poll-timeout now carries a resumeToken, and session.resumePoll(token) continues the same transaction. The token is plain JSON that survives a restart, it carries no secret, and it grants nothing: every response on the resumed poll is protection-verified and nonce-bound, and the grant is held to the key the token names, exactly as the first process did.

Added: A pki.cmp.session poll-timeout verdict carries resumeToken, and session.resumePoll(token) continues that transaction in a later process. The token is plain JSON, so it survives being written to disk and read back: it names the transaction identifier the exchange is keyed by, the nonce the next request must echo (RFC 9810 section 5.1.1), which request is being polled as a decimal string so an identifier of any width survives, the response arm its grant arrives on, the polls already spent, the public key the granted certificate must certify, the signer identity the first process authenticated and, separately, the certificate it currently verifies a response with when that response omits its extraCerts, the certificates the authority had already sent including any it delivered only on a waiting leg, and the instant its own checkAfter allows the next poll. It carries no secret, because the protection material, the trust anchors and the endpoint come from the session the caller builds to resume with. It grants nothing either: the resumed poll protection-verifies and nonce-binds every response before reading it, holds every response to the signer identity the token names, refuses a granted certificate that certifies a different key, and confirms the grant with the same certConf handshake, so a token is state rather than authority. Those fields are what the resumed session holds the exchange to, so a token is integrity-sensitive and belongs in storage the caller controls: someone who can rewrite it can widen what the resumed session accepts, up to the limit of that session's own trust anchors and the authority's protection, which a rewritten token cannot reach past. Store it where the enrollment's own state is stored, and read it back into a session built from the same credentials. The authority's polling interval is waited out before the first resumed request, while the resuming session's own maxTotalWait still bounds it: a remainder longer than that budget times out immediately and hands the same due time on. A further timeout returns another token, so a wait can span any number of processes, and the polls each one spent accumulate across them. The two fields that bind the transaction are required rather than optional, since a token lives in storage where it can be edited and dropping a field must not drop the check it feeds: the key the grant is held to, and, for a signature session, the identity every response is held to. A shared-secret session pins no certificate, and its secret is the binding instead. A token that is not an object, names no transaction, carries a non-hex identifier or non-canonical base64 nonce, names a response arm that is not an enrollment arm, omits a binding field, carries an unknown field, names a key that is not a SubjectPublicKeyInfo, carries a field that is not a certificate, or carries more certificates than the list it restores is built under (the authority's pool keeps the response bounds, while the chain that validates the signer is held to the path length and the codec, since it can carry an opts.intermediates certificate that never crossed the wire) is refused with cmp/bad-input before any request is sent, so stored state that cannot be used never spends the nonce the token is the only copy of, and a session that has already run a transaction refuses to resume one, since RFC 9810 section 5.1.1 gives each transaction its own identifier.
